title: Shade for the Busiest Bus Stops

before.title: Water at the Bus Stop
before.text: This town is not real. Its hot days make bus stops hard to use. The town cannot build a big roof at every stop. People mark the stops used most on a map. Workers add shade and water there first. They plant trees where the roots will not block the path.

after.title: Shade for the Busiest Bus Stops
after.text: This town is imagined. On hot days, people wait in the sun at its bus stops. The town cannot add shade everywhere at once. Workers count how many people use each stop. They put a small shelter at one busy stop with enough space beside the path. At another stop, they plan a tree where its roots and branches will not block people. They return the next week to check both places.

reason: The made-up town’s mapping, water and tree work had been classed as explanatory nonfiction. Mark as fiction, remove unexplained drinking-water provision, and distinguish an installed shelter from a planned tree whose shade would take time. The visit and follow-up are a bounded invented process.

title: How a Cup Telephone Carries Sound

before.title: Sound from a String
before.text: Kai pulls a string tight between two cups. He speaks into one cup while Mei holds the other. His voice makes the first cup move a little. The string carries that movement to the second cup. It makes the air there move, and Mei hears Kai's words.

after.title: How a Cup Telephone Carries Sound
after.text: Kai and Mei connect two cups with a string. They pull it tight. Kai speaks into one cup while Mei holds the other near her ear. His voice makes the bottom of Kai’s cup vibrate. The string carries that vibration to Mei’s cup. The second cup vibrates and moves the air near her ear. Mei hears his words. If the string hangs loose, the sound does not travel as well.

reason: The original omitted that the cups are joined and that the string must stay tight. The checked Exploratorium activity describes voice vibrations moving from cup to taut string to the second cup and air at the listener’s ear. The ending correctly limits performance when the string is loose.
